💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, volkswagen revealed the ID.
  • We knew Volkswagen was cooking something “really spicy” up after teasing the newly introduced GTI hot hatch earlier this week.
  • Volkswagen launched the first-generation Golf GTI in 1976, which essentially defined the hot hatch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, volkswagen revealed the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, an electric pocket rocket with a massive rear wing and 362 horsepower.

We knew Volkswagen was cooking something “really spicy” up after teasing the newly introduced GTI hot hatch earlier this week.

Volkswagen launched the first-generation Golf GTI in 1976, which essentially defined the hot hatch. To celebrate the brand’s legendary performance badge, a signature of its sporty, practical hatchbacks, VW is entering a latest era with its first fully electric GTI.

The GTI has been “one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years,” Volkswagen’s technical development boss, Kai Grünitz, remarked.

After opening pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, the brand’s first EV to wear the badge, Volkswagen introduced the Clubsport Concept, a souped-up two-door electric pocket rocket.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept demonstrates “how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world,” according to Grünitz.

According to recent reports, it’s based on the production ID. Polo GTI uses the same MEB+ platform, but VW reengineered it with a larger electric motor to pump out more power.

According to recent reports, the Clubsport is powered by a 362 hp (270 kW) front-mounted electric motor (APP550) that’s typically used in the rear of VW’s larger EVs, like the ID. Tiguan and the ID.7. That’s up considerably from the 233 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft of torque of the standard ID. Polo GTI offers.

Thomas Schmall, CEO of Volkswagen Group Components, said the APP550 motor is “one of the most efficient electric drives in its class.”.

According to recent reports, thanks to an electronically controlled front differential lock (VAQ), Volkswagen said, the Clubsport version can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 4.7 seconds, beating the standard ID. Polo GTI by a full two seconds (6.8 seconds).

Volkswagen also fine-tuned the adaptive chassis control (DCC) to make it racetrack-ready and added new ceramic brakes to help slow it down.

The Clubsport version uses the same 52 kW NMC battery as the ID. Polo GTI, which can provide up to 389 hp (290 kW), Volkswagen said, enabling a top speed of 149 mph (240 km/h).

According to recent reports, on the exterior, the Clubsport is a two-door model rather than a four-door. It’s 100 mm longer than the standard ID. Polo GTI, with each wing flared an additional 50 mm. It also gets a large motorsport splitter up front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser, and a massive carbon-fiber rear wing.

Inside, the cabin is tailored to the racetrack with a minimalist, stripped-down, two-seater layout. As such, there’s no infotainment system, just a center display to switch between drive modes.

The dash panel, side trims, and other interior elements feature dark ArtVelours microfibre with red topstitching, reinforcing the racetrack-ready interior.

Industry observers note that following the ID. Polo GTI, new ID.3 GTI, and Golf GTI Edition 50, the new ID. Polo Clubsport is the fourth model to debut this year under the performance badge.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000). In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

And American compact car enthusiasts drool over more unobtanium.

The company will showcase the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport concept car at the Essen Motor Show next week, starting on November 27.

Volkswagen didn’t confirm prepares to launch a production version, but don’t expect it to reach the States.

According to recent reports, the standard VW ID. Polo and GTI are not sold in the US, so the souped-up Clubsport variant likely won’t be either. Hopefully, VW changes its mind and proves us wrong.

Wild Conversations With Animals Foster Humility and Harmony

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • I'm always looking for books that foster a strong sense of community and connection with nonhuman animals.
  • Industry observers note that susan Beilby Magee: I wrote it because I made a promise to a lion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

I'm always looking for books that foster a strong sense of community and connection with nonhuman animals. This is just what author Susan Beilby Magee does in her new book Wild Conversations: The Wisdom of African Animals, in which she shares wisdom and illuminates a path toward resilience, purpose, and harmony for all of Earth’s inhabitants. She also offers pertinent data from detailed research. Many of her positive messages reminded me of an interview I did with George Bumann about how eavesdropping on the wild conversations with different animals can offer lessons on the remarkable beings they are and what they need from us.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Wild Conversations?

Industry observers note that susan Beilby Magee: I wrote it because I made a promise to a lion. During a safari in northern Tanzania, I encountered a magnificent male lion walking through the bush. I greeted him silently and received a question in the intuitive way I have communicated with animals for decades: “Will you write a book about us? Will you share our messages with other humans?” I mentioned: “Yes.”.

In a recent development, that promise deepened over three African safaris. Their messages were wise, sometimes humorous, but grew urgent as wilderness habitats shrank. For example, lions have disappeared from more than 90 percent of their historic range, and research shows that only about 25 percent of Africa’s savannahs remain within the range of free-ranging lion populations. I wanted readers to encounter these animals not merely as tourist attractions on a safari, but as fellow beings with their own families, awareness, and place on Mother Earth. This book honors that promise.

Industry observers note that SBM: I hope to reach animal lovers, conservationists, travelers, people curious about spirituality, and anyone who has felt renewed spending time in nature. I want to reach people overwhelmed by modern life. You need not believe in animal telepathy to recognize the intelligence and dignity of the animals. Although pollution, poaching, and human expansion threaten them, conservation can reverse some of the damage. For example, in Chad’s Zakouma National Park, where poaching had devastated the elephants, only one calf was counted in 2011. In 2018, due to intervention and protection by African Parks, 127 calves were counted. I want my granddaughter’s generation to see what is at stake. I hope readers finish with wonder, affection, and a desire to protect the wild.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

SBM: The book takes readers from the Serengeti and Tarangire to Ruaha and the Okavango Delta. I share personal encounters and photographs that explore animal wisdom, family life, interconnectedness, spiritual awareness, and conservation.

Sources indicate that our jeep once approached a herd of more than 200 elephants. The matriarch stopped, watched us, and directed the herd to surround the youngest calves. When I silently asked for her message, I heard: “Slow down. Don’t rush. Enjoy the moment. Love your family. Play together. Know that you, we, all life is eternal.” How many of us need a reminder to slow down? The message was not just a comfort, but also a warning: When we move as fast as so many of us do today, we often miss what really matters, whether it’s time with loved ones or confronting the harm we’re causing to the planet.

Other animals offered different lessons. A giraffe invited me to appreciate silence. A leopard encouraged spending time alone in nature and trusting our own inner resources. The hyenas urged purposeful work and devotion to one’s pack. And the lions reminded me to awaken my senses, appreciate beauty, and live with courage. Each message reflected its messenger.

Industry observers note that there is also a harder truth: Life and death are interconnected. I watched wildebeest cross the Mara River as crocodiles waited, while predators, scavengers and insects each played a role. Death is natural. What we are doing to these animals is not.

In the book’s final section, Clarion Call, the messages become urgent. Habitat loss, pollution, and human expansion threaten these animals. I worry that lions, elephants, cheetahs and other magnificent creatures may disappear from the wild within my granddaughter’s lifetime. The population of Africa’s savanna elephants has fallen by at least 60 percent in 50 years, according to the IUCN. My central appeal is both spiritual and practical: Reconnect with Mother Earth, recognize that we belong to the same living community, and act to protect the places these animals call home.

MB: How does your book differ from others concerned with similar topics?

It has been revealed that SBM: Wild Conversations is neither a scientific field guide nor a conventional safari memoir. I write as a modern mystic, sharing the messages I personally experienced through silent, intuitive communication with animals. Readers may interpret these encounters differently; I welcome that. I simply invite them to pay attention.

The foreword is by Michael Lorentz, a wildlife photographer who has guided African safaris for 40 years. He writes that the animals are “far more present, far more aware, and far more communicative than most of us are conditioned to believe.” Frank Pope, CEO of Save the Elephants, has endorsed the book, calling it “A passionate love-letter to the wild.” You don’t have to be a mystic to appreciate the book’s photographs and messages.

MB: Are you hopeful that learning more about these animals will inspire greater action to save them and the African wilderness?

Industry observers note that SBM: Yes. I hope people will protect wild animals and wilderness worldwide. When we watch an elephant protect her calf or lion cubs tumble together in play, the distance between “us” and “them” begins to disappear. We see families, relationships, and individual lives. That recognition can lead to respect, and respect can lead to stewardship. I want my granddaughter and all future generations to inherit a world where wild lions still roar, elephants still roam, and the Serengeti remains alive with migrating herds.

A leader in Seattle’s women’s movement in the 1970s, she served as a White House Fellow under President Gerald Ford and later became an international business consultant. She holds an MBA from the Wharton School and a BA from Pomona College.

It has been revealed that this is adorable and I want one. Hedley Studios in the UK just came out with a replica Porsche 550 Spyder, which itself isn't a unique idea. There have been Volkswagen-powered 550 Spyder replicas for decades. What sets this one apart are two things: one is that it's only 80% scale, so it's a little fella, and the other is that it's electric. It's called the Porsche 550 J (for Junior) it looks like a blast.

In a recent development, I can't tell if the 550 J is a track toy or just a toy, but either way it looks like fun. At 80% scale, it looks positively bite-sized next to the real one, which was already one of the smallest production road cars you'll ever see. So it's tiny. So much so, in fact, that I struggle to see how two adults can actually fit in its two seats side-by-side. And, as you'd imagine with such a tiny footprint, the 550 J isn't road legal and is only meant for private roads and race track.

According to recent reports, like a real 550 Spyder, all of the 550 J's weight is behind the driver. Two 1.8 kWh battery packs provide the juice at 48 volts, while a single 11 horsepower electric motor drives the rear wheels. It only weighs 728 pounds, so that power should be enough to have some fun with. Add two passengers, though, and its weight can pretty easily pass the half-ton mark. At that point, 11 horses isn't much. However, there is an optional RS pack that bumps it to 21 horsepower. Top speed also jumps from 40 mph to 50 mph.

The RS Pack also adds two more of those 1.8 kWh battery packs, though, which adds another 44 pounds. That weight penalty might be worth it for the range, though. The standard 550 J only has 30 miles of range, while the RS has 50. That isn't a lot but it's enough for a track day. Plus, with such small batteries, the 550 J will charge up rapidly. Lap the track a bunch of times, plug it in and have some lunch, and get back to it.

Recent findings suggest that track days should be fun, too. Bilstein dampers with Eibach springs handle suspension duty, while Brembo brakes do the stopping. The RS model gets Bilstein adjustable coilovers and drilled brake rotors, too. So despite having Power Wheels-levels of horsepower, it has genuine track car handling bits.

Hedley has done an admirable job of making the 550 J look like a real 550 Spyder that was hit with a shrink ray. It's smaller, sure, but you wouldn't know it from photos. Everything about it looks spot on, from every exterior detail of its carbon fiber body, to the interior switchgear, and even the fuel filler cap. It's a very impressive recreation and one that will look fantastic in owners' garages. Hedley claims it worked closely with the Porsche Museum to get all the details right and it shows.

In a recent development, only 250 of these will be made, and they'll cost £69,500 ($91,406) each. So it isn't cheap, especially for something that isn't road legal. However, for folks who can afford to spend that kind of cash on a track day toy, this seems like a really fun way to do it.

The time has arrived for another Arc Raiders revision, and Embark has certainly delivered. Today’s patch, version 1.6.0, is among the smallest the game has received so far, focusing almost exclusively on disabling map exploits.

Perhaps more important than the patch itself, however, is the announcement the developer made around it.

Starting off with patch 1.6.0, it takes out a particular zipline on Stella Montis, the game’s most recent addition ot the map roster. Some players used said zipline to get out of bounds, something the game has been battling on several of its maps.

On Blue Gate, the patch fixes a collision concern that allowed players to vault through a wall, and fall to their death. The map fixes continue with another on Spaceport Launch Tower, which takes out a gap in collision that players have been able to shoot through.

In a recent development, the last change in this update affects gameplay feel around Arc enemies. Certain materials in the game’s world weren’t blocking their vision - or fire - when they should have, and this has now been fixed.

Alongside today’s patch, Embark also announced that going forward, we’re going to see fewer patches for Arc Raiders. The game has been getting updates almost every Thursday since it released in late October.

Now that most of the major problems have been fixed, the studio is shifting to a slower patching cadence. Critical fixes will still be issued as soon as they’re developed, but don’t expect a patch each week going forward.

Recent findings suggest that embark also revealed that patch releases and in-game store rotations will now occur on Tuesdays. You should also expect the next few weeks to be quiet, as members of the team go on holiday breaks.

Recent findings suggest that but, before everyone goes away, the game is going to get one more significant revision. The last item on Arc Raiders’ roadmap, revealed in early November, is the Cold Snap event. This is on track for Tuesday, bringing some new content alongside a few other fixes.

Does Menopausal Hormone Therapy Lower Dementia Risk? Timing and Genetics May Hold the Answer

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a newly introduced study.
  • The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.
  • The findings could offer new insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a newly introduced study.

The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.

The findings could offer new insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.

Researchers also found that certain associations between hormone therapy and brain health differed depending on whether women carried a genetic variant associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

However, the relationship between estrogen and brain health is complex. While the findings suggest that longer estrogen exposure may be associated with healthier brain aging, they do not establish that hormone therapy can prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

The researchers drew data from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort, a longitudinal study of 1,203 individuals born in 1944 who resided in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The final cohort included 352 cisgender women, with an average age of 70, who had no neurological disorders and reliable self-reported data on their estrogen exposure.

According to recent reports, individual estrogen exposure was measured through structured interviews. It included:.

The researchers used this information as a proxy for lifetime estrogen exposure, though the study didn’t measure actual hormone levels.

Participants were also given a brain MRI at baseline and then again at a 5-year follow-up.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that those with a longer reproductive span had a lower risk of small vessel disease (SVD). Participants with a longer reproductive life span had an 8% lower risk of having two or more signs of SVD. However, later menopause, rather than earlier menstruation, appeared to be the main driver of this association.

Those who used MHT also tended to have fewer signs of SVD and better microstructural integrity in the white matter.

Sources indicate that in individuals who carried the APOE-ε4 variant, which increases a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease, MHT was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease. However, there was no association for those without this variant.

The researchers noted that longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that estrogen has several key effects on the brain that may help support cognitive health.

It influences communication between brain cells, supports the brain’s ability to use glucose for energy, helps regulate neurotransmitters, and plays a role in maintaining healthy blood vessels and reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

Recent findings suggest that “As estrogen levels decline during menopause, some of these protective effects may diminish. Replacing estrogen closer to the menopause transition could potentially help preserve some of these functions during a vulnerable period for brain health,” he mentioned. “While these findings are encouraging, MHT has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.”.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed and noted, “Starting menopausal hormone therapy earlier in the menopause transition may help minimize some changes by supporting the brain during this period of hormonal fluctuation.”.

“There is growing interest in whether early estrogen therapy may also help reduce the long-term risk of Alzheimer’s disease, although more research is needed before we can establish that benefit,” she added.

Ross told Healthline that this research reinforces the importance of recognizing menopause as more than a reproductive or hormonal transition.

Sources indicate that “We know that women are disproportionately affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and some women experience noticeable cognitive changes beginning in perimenopause,” she said. “If future research confirms that starting hormone therapy earlier can help protect long-term cognitive health, it could influence how we approach menopause treatment and encourage more proactive conversations between women and their healthcare providers.”.

“The goal should be to individualize treatment based on a woman’s symptoms, medical history, and overall health rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach,” Ross added.

Trinh agreed that an individualized approach to menopause management is notable.

“This does not mean that every woman should start hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Instead, it highlights the importance of understanding which women might benefit, when treatment should begin, and which formulations are most appropriate,” he noted. “Factors such as age, time since menopause, cardiovascular risk, metabolic health, family history, and potentially genetic factors may all help guide future recommendations.”.

“We still need stronger clinical evidence before changing current prescribing guidelines specifically for dementia prevention,” Trinh added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, italy’s transport ministry has granted provisional approval to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” in Europe. Italy becomes the 12th European country to allow the system, and the first of the EU’s major markets.

Recent findings suggest that it also didn’t wait for Brussels. The EU committee that decides on bloc-wide recognition isn’t expected to vote until December at the earliest.

Industry observers note that deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini revealed the decision on X on Friday. He wrote that the ministry (MIT) gave the green light after a “thorough technical feasibility check,” and that Italy is getting ahead of the EU recognition process, which he described as “still being defined.”.

Tesla Europe followed with a one-liner, “Now approved in Italy, rollout begins soon,” and a video of one of its cars driving itself through Rome. There’s no firm rollout date yet.

Sources indicate that it’s still a Level 2 driver-assist system. It can steer, brake, accelerate, and handle intersections and lane changes, but the driver has to supervise at all times and stays fully responsible for the car.

It has been revealed that the Dutch vehicle authority RDW was first, approving FSD Supervised on April 10 under Article 39 of the EU type-approval regulation. Other member states can then recognize that approval nationally, one by one.

Ten did before Italy: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Those are mostly small markets. Together with the Netherlands, they add up to about 70 million people, or roughly 15% of the EU’s population.

Italy alone has about 59 million people, so Friday’s decision nearly doubles the share of Europeans who can legally use the system, to close to 30%.

Rome’s position moved fast. In April, Senator Carlo Calenda formally asked Salvini’s ministry to prioritize the approval. On October 29, Salvini posted that he’d had a “very positive and constructive” call with Elon Musk and that Italy supported a “swift EU approval,” which read at the time as backing for an EU-level decision, not a national one. Three weeks later, Italy went national.

A lot changed in between. Tesla dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe after Germany’s Transport Ministry called it misleading, and cut the maximum speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit. Then on November 16, the RDW approved stricter driver monitoring, including hands on the wheel above 130 km/h. That’s the version Italy is approving.

The EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) pushed the Tesla vote to December after holding only discussions in October. Bloc-wide approval needs a qualified majority: at least 15 of 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU population.

According to recent reports, germany remarked in October it would back approval after Tesla agreed to the rename and the speed cap. If it follows through, Germany and the 12 approving countries would cover roughly 47% of the EU’s population.

That’s progress for Tesla, but it’s not 65%. France refused a national approval in July, and Spain hasn’t recognized the Dutch approval. Tesla needs at least one of them, plus most of the remaining holdouts.

According to recent reports, I used FSD for five days this past week. It's impressive on controlled roads.

Even in Chill driving mode, there were still more than a few times that I had to use the Critical feedback.

In a recent development, to think it will ever be perfect is pure fantasy. I will never climb into a automobile that does not have steering controls.

Sources indicate that seven repairs and $10,000 on a leaky roof in two years, with no guarantees. When you factor in Musk, I'm done.

Both Carmax and OnlyUsedTesla acknowledged receiving my requests. No offers from either service 48-hours later. Guess I'm not the only one that's done with Tesla.

In a recent development, this is a real win for Tesla, and for Italian owners with HW4 cars who have been paying for a feature they couldn’t use at home. Italy is Tesla’s first big European market to say yes, and it shifts momentum going into December.

But it’s pretty crazy that now Europe is going to get a safer FSD than in the US.

I bet that this will get reflected in the data, if we ever get to see it.

Tech Report: Why Does Life Feel Absurd?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • “MOST people feel on occasion that life is absurd, and some feel it vividly and continually” is how Thomas Nagel opens his paper "The Absurd," yet "they could not really explain why life is absurd.
  • As Albert Camus is most often associated with the term the absurd, I will begin with his account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

“MOST people feel on occasion that life is absurd, and some feel it vividly and continually” is how Thomas Nagel opens his paper "The Absurd," yet "they could not really explain why life is absurd. Why then do they provide a natural expression for the sense that it is?” This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

What then is the absurd? As Albert Camus is most often associated with the term the absurd, I will begin with his account. He begins by illustrating the common uses of the word absurd and gives the example of a virtuous man, who we accuse of desiring his sister. Naturally, he would respond in shock: “That is absurd!” Thereby appealing to the “contradictory” and “impossible” notion of the accusation, like a man attacking a group of gunmen with a sword. The intention of the action clashes with the harsh reality, thereby rendering the whole endeavor absurd. For Camus, the “absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need [for meaning and reason] and the unreasonable silence of the world.”.

The feeling of the absurd therefore stems from two realizations taken together. First, man’s realization that life is meaningless and the universe purposeless; and secondly, man’s desire for meaning and purpose. The absurd is the futile search for meaning. It is neither existential nihilism that is absurd, nor the human search for meaning, but the comparison, the conflict, that arises between them.

Recent findings suggest that let us now take a look at an analytical philosopher, i.e., Thomas Nagel and his paper “The Absurd." Nagel, too, starts from the notion of the absurd in ordinary life, giving a similar analysis to Camus’, stating that it “includes a conspicuous discrepancy between pretension or aspiration and reality," like someone giving a complex speech on a vote that has already been cast. A philosophical notion of absurdity, in contrast to the feeling of absurdity, however, must according to Nagel lie in “something universal-some respect in which pretension and reality inevitably clash for us all” and that is a “collision between the seriousness with which we take our lives and the perpetual possibility of regarding everything about which we are serious as arbitrary, or open to doubt.”.

As one might argue goes, “why struggle, if the struggle doesn’t amount to anything?” This question is unique for humans, in that only they have the ability to take a step back and look at themselves from a grander point of view, which is seemingly impossible for animals. From this perspective, our lives must appear “sobering and comical.” As Nagel claims:.

We step back to find that the whole system of justification and criticism, which controls our choices and supports our claims to rationality, rests on responses and habits that we never question, that we should not know how to defend without circularity, and to which we shall continue to adhere even after they are called into question.

According to recent reports, our aims and goals must from this perspective appear arbitrary. They are, in the end, so small and insignificant that one can only wonder why we put so much energy into achieving our life goals. This is the absurd condition we cannot escape.

We must, therefore, acknowledge that the “absurdity of our situation derives not from a collision between our expectations and the world, but from a collision within ourselves.” I don’t agree with Nagel, in his claim to provide a superior account to that of Camus. If anything, Nagel reinforces Camus’ argument. For Camus as for Nagel, the search for final justifications in God, religion, power, family or the state is just as futile, for their purposes must appear just as absurd if we take a step back. They are no more than an escape from the absurd, not a solution. For now, it seems as if Camus’ notion of the absurd is compatible with contemporary analytical philosophy after all.

Industry News: Early Americans spent over 10 hours making a single pumpkin pie

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table.
  • According to recent reports, it seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert.
  • For generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table. The flesh has been cooked until soft. But the hard part is still ahead. To turn the pumpkin into pie, the cook must mash it, scrape it, and force it through a sieve, separating smooth pulp from stubborn strings and fibers. There is no can of pumpkin puree. No food processor. Just the pumpkin, rudimentary kitchen tools, and a lot of elbow grease. The work could take hours, all for an eight-person dessert. An 1876 Fresh England cookbook, for example, instructed cooks to simmer pumpkin for six to eight hours, stirring frequently, before rubbing it through a colander.

According to recent reports, it seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert. Pumpkin flesh doesn’t naturally break down into a silky puree. Cooking softens its tissues, but turning the squash into smooth filling requires additional mechanical work.

For generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle. Eventually, factories took over the work of cooking and processing pumpkins into puree. But the solution didn’t stop there. Growers also turned to pumpkin varieties with naturally smoother, less fibrous flesh, making the job easier before the squash even reached the factory.

It has been revealed that pumpkin was an key food in North America long before Thanksgiving became a national holiday. Indigenous peoples cultivated and prepared the squash in many forms, and European colonists adopted pumpkins as a plentiful crop. Colonists adapted their own pie-making traditions to the abundant squash, incorporating pumpkin into sweet and savory pies. By the 17th century, recipes for pumpkin-filled pies were appearing in English cookbooks.

In 1796, the first known American cookbook, Amelia Simmons’s American Cookery, included a recipe for “Pompkin Pudding” made with cooked pumpkin, milk, eggs, and spices. Before the pumpkin could be combined with the other ingredients, the recipe called for it to be strained, separating fine pulp from tougher material.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving didn’t take shape as a national tradition until the mid-19th century. Pumpkins were harvested in the fall and could be stored through the colder months, making them a natural ingredient for a holiday associated with the autumn harvest.

The story of the Pilgrims sitting down with Native Americans for the first Thanksgiving has some truth to it, too. In 1621, English colonists and members of the Wampanoag people did gather for a three-day harvest celebration. But the friendly, feel-good version passed down in schoolbooks leaves out a much more complicated history of colonialism and conflict.

It wasn’t until over two centuries later that Sarah Josepha Hale, a prominent magazine editor, campaigned for decades for a national holiday, and, in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national “day of Thanksgiving.” She believed a shared day of gratitude, centered on family and community, could help unite a country increasingly divided by political conflict.

According to recent reports, hale also helped popularize the foods associated with the holiday, promoting a traditional Fresh England Thanksgiving menu through her magazine. Pumpkin pie was already a regional favorite, but as Thanksgiving spread nationally after the Civil War, the dessert became part of the broader American tradition.

Industry observers note that pumpkin pie became increasingly associated with the holiday meal during this era, drawing on its roots in Latest England’s seasonal cooking traditions. Preparing it remained labor-intensive, and results varied.

Industrial food processing offered a solution to the labor-intensive process of making pumpkin pie. Factories could cook and mechanically break down pumpkin in large quantities, producing puree without requiring every household to repeat the tedious process. Canning transformed pumpkin from a seasonal ingredient demanding considerable preparation into a convenient product that could be stored and used when needed.

John Coupland, Ph.D., professor of food science at Penn State, describes the work involved in preparing pumpkin by hand as “astonishing.” Industrial processing made pie filling far more convenient, eliminating the need to cook, mash, and strain a pumpkin from scratch.

It also gave bakers a reliable starting point, helping make pumpkin pie more consistent and cementing its place at the Thanksgiving table.

Sources indicate that making pumpkin puree is more complicated than simply cooking the flesh until soft. Pumpkin cells are surrounded by walls containing materials such as cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Cooking softens the tissue, while mechanical processing breaks it into smaller particles. Together, these processes help determine the puree’s texture and moisture.

The goal is a smooth puree that is neither watery nor full of tough fibers. The pumpkin variety matters, as do the heating conditions and mechanical methods used to break down its flesh.

In a recent development, modern food processing allows manufacturers to control these variables on a large scale, producing batches with similar textures and moisture levels. That predictability is especially valuable in pumpkin pie, where the filling’s consistency helps determine the finished dessert.

But the food industry found another way to improve the process: start with a pumpkin better suited to the job.

That is where Libby’s, one of the country’s largest canned-pumpkin producers, and the Dickinson pumpkin enter the story.

According to Libby’s, farmer Elijah Dickinson brought special Dickinson pumpkin seeds from Kentucky to Illinois in 1835. The variety became closely associated with commercial pumpkin processing, and Libby, McNeill & Libby acquired Dickinson & Co. in 1929, strengthening the company’s connection to the crop.

Dickinson pumpkins look different from the bright orange pumpkins sold for carving (often called field pumpkins). Their tan skin matters less to processors than the dense flesh beneath it. Relatively high in solids and sugars, Dickinson pumpkins are particularly well-suited to puree.

Many carving pumpkins, by contrast, have stringier flesh that makes them harder to process into a smooth puree. Coupland explains that they are not ideally suited to commercial food production because their fibers can be difficult to break down.

Sources indicate that coupland describes Dickinson puree as having a “smooth, even texture,” adding that it means you won’t be “picking fibers out of your teeth.” Rather than trying to eliminate the stringiness of a carving pumpkin, processors can start with a variety whose natural characteristics make the job easier. The raw material itself becomes part of the technology.

Libby’s helped bring this approach into American kitchens through its canned-pumpkin business, pairing a suitable variety with industrial processing to deliver consistent puree to home bakers.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Dickinson pumpkins belong to Cucurbita moschata, a species that includes several varieties of winter squash. Many familiar carving pumpkins belong to Cucurbita pepo. Botanically, the distinction between pumpkin and squash is largely a matter of common usage rather than a strict scientific boundary. The FDA permits certain sweet, golden-fleshed squashes to be labeled as pumpkin in canned products, reflecting the longstanding overlap in how the terms are used in the food trade.

It has been revealed that for pumpkin pie, what matters most is the flesh inside: how it tastes, how it breaks down, and how consistently it performs. Today’s Thanksgiving cooks no longer needs to work themselves to the bone because the food industry has learned to do the work first.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hyundai and Kia have some of the strongest hybrid lineups on the market. Why did it take so long for Genesis to get there?

Industry observers note that hyundai and Kia hybrids are printing money. Hybrids now account for 29% of all Hyundai sales, a proportion that has grown rapidly over the last few years. But Genesis has so far been left out of the hybrid sales bonanza. No longer. Genesis revealed the G80 and GV80 hybrids on Wednesday, finally entering the fast-growing market for premium hybrids.

It has been revealed that the G80 and GV80 are the Genesis brand’s mid-size sedan and SUV, respectively. The G80 competes against cars like the BMW 5 Series and Mercedes E-Class and was—until recently—offered with a fully electric powertrain. That was canned after slow sales, and the GV80 SUV has always been internal-combustion only.

Sources indicate that both models come standard with a 2.5-liter turbocharged gas engine and offer twin-turbo V-6 engines as performance upgrades. The new hybrid system will slot between these two powertrains. It adds a parallel hybrid setup to the 2.5-liter turbocharged powertrain, delivering a combined total of 347 horsepower. The top-trim V6 produces 375 hp, for reference.

In a recent development, genesis claims the GV80 Hybrid is 24% more efficient than the four-cylinder gas model. For that G80 Hybrid, that number is 30%. Final fuel economy ratings are still to come, but that’s a sizable improvement given the extra power it comes with. And like their gas-powered siblings, all G80s and GV80s come with all-wheel-drive.

All G80 and GV80 Hybrids come standard with all-wheel drive.

Recent findings suggest that kind of. The 2.5T turbo-hybrid combo is used in other Hyundai products like the Palisade Hybrid, but it is among the newest, most sophisticated powerplants in the company’s stable. But the G80 and GV80 do get some Genesis-exclusive hardware. The Genesis hybrids are the first Hyundai Motor Group (HMG) hybrids to feature liquid-cooled batteries. The vast majority of traditional hybrids use small batteries that are passively air-cooled, but as we know from larger EV batteries, active cooling systems are great for long-term stability. Genesis notes the cooling system also allows it to take advantage of more of the battery’s energy.

Recent findings suggest that fundamentally, though, the powertrain should feel similar to existing Hyundai and Kia hybrids. Unlike Honda and Toyota hybrids, HMG hybrids still use traditional transmissions rather than e-CVTs. The G80 and GV80 use a seven-speed automatic, rather than the eight-speed auto that’s employed on the gas models.

The upcoming models offer a “Stay” mode that allows you to run the HVAC and radio for extended periods without firing the gas engine, too, and an EV mode for a limited amount of engine-off cruising.

If you want something that’s more similar to an EV driving experience, Genesis already makes two smaller electric SUVs, the GV60 and Electrified GV70. A third one, the stunning GV90, is coming soon.

But if you want something like a plug-in hybrid, you’ll have to wait for the company’s extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs). EREVs—which use gasoline engines purely as generators, with no direct mechanical between the engine and wheels—are coming in 2027, Genesis confirmed at the debut event. The company claims they will offer over 640 miles of combined range. EREV fans will have to wait for further details.

The rear seat of the top-trim Genesis G80 Hybrid.

Industry observers note that but if you’re a pure hybrid fan, Genesis finally has a couple of real options. Pricing, trim details, and on-sale dates are still to come. Expect to hear more details next year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest Renault Twingo E-Tech is among the most affordable vehicles, electric or gas-powered, starting at just £14,745 in the UK, or under $20,000.

Another affordable, practical EV the US will never see. Renault’s fresh Twingo E-Tech is an electric remake of its iconic 1990s city car.

It has been revealed that the retro-looking EV went on sale in Europe earlier this year, starting at under €20,000 ($22,000), before government incentives. In places like Germany, it starts at about €13,990 ($15,500), including the €6,000 ($6,600) federal EV grant.

In the UK, Renault announced that prices for the Twingo E-Tech will start at just £14,745, or about $19,500. That includes the government’s Electric Clean Car Grant (ECG) of £3,750 ($4,900).

At that price, Renault’s upcoming electric car is among the most affordable vehicles available, including gas-powered cars.

It has been revealed that it’s cheaper than the gas-powered Dacia Sandero (£14,765) and BYD’s cheapest EV, the Dolphin Surf (£18,675). Only a few cars are lower-priced, including the Dacia Spring (£11,990) and Leapmotor T03 (£12,995).

What do you get for the price? At just 3,790 mm (149.2″) long, the electric city car is a bit smaller than the Hyundai Inster and the BYD Dolphin Surf.

For those in the US, that’s even smaller than the first-generation Chevy Bolt EV, which measured 4,145 mm (163.2″) in length.

Despite its compact size, the “cheeky, practical” 5-door city car, as Renault calls it, offers up to 360 liters of boot capacity. It also features independent, sliding 50/50 folding rear seats to haul bigger items like a surfboard.

With up to 50 kW DC fast charging, Renault mentioned the Twingo E-Tech can charge from 15% to 80% in 28 minutes.

The base Renault Twingo E-Tech Evolution, priced from £14,745 ($19,500), uses a 27.5 kWh LFP battery and an 80 hp (60 kW) motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range.

The entry-level version features 16″ steel wheels, a 7″ driver display, 10″ navigation screen, and ADAS features, including cruise control and lane-keep assist.

Renault will offer three Twingo E-Tech trims in total. The mid-range Techno trim gains 18″ wheels, Google built-in with Renault’s Reno avatar, a reversing camera, automatic climate control, a hands-free key card, One Pedal driving, and heated front seats. It starts at £16,245 ($21,500), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG.

With Google built in, drivers can easily find and navigate to charging stations via Google Maps, use Google Gemini AI virtual assistance, or access over 100 apps, including Waze and Amazon Music.

At least this car has some styling unlike the generic box style VW offerings in this category. In this size car I prefer the SUV style of the Dacia Spring for myself, but of course we will never see any of these wonderful cars in the USA.

The top-spec Twingo E-Tech Launch Edition, priced from £17,645 ($23,200), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG, adds a suite of ADAS features, including blind-spot warning, rear cross-traffic alert and hands-free parking.

Inside, the Launch Edition features a special mottled textile upholstery with red stitching and premium floor mats.

Renault is offering a special promo for those who buy a new Twingo E-Tech through Mobilize Financial Services on a PCP or HP agreement by June 30, 2027, which includes two years’ free servicing.

Interested buyers can purchase the Twingo R Pass for £100, giving them priority access to ordering, a mini Twingo E-Tech model, and a green Renault key cover.

#63773. The Ache of Feeling Overlooked

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (996 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Ache of Feeling Overlooked

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Recent findings suggest that we never really know what someone else is carrying in their backpack of rocks.
  • Younger doctors would seek her out after shifts and, though she never gave much overt advice, when she spoke they paid attention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Recent findings suggest that we never really know what someone else is carrying in their backpack of rocks. One of my former colleagues, a brilliant consultant, springs to mind. She was highly experienced, calmly present under pressure, and one of those people a hospital comes to depend upon without anyone saying as much.

Younger doctors would seek her out after shifts and, though she never gave much overt advice, when she spoke they paid attention. Usually she listened carefully, asked a question, or helped them see what had just happened from a new perspective. She was also the last person who would have wanted a fuss made of her.

Sources indicate that at some point, she started to change. Nothing dramatic, and she still came to work and took care of her patients as diligently and professionally as ever. If you'd asked me then whether anything was noticeably wrong, I am embarrassed to admit that I would probably have dismissed it. On reflection, I can see that she'd stopped staying behind after teaching sessions to chat with students. She also spoke less in meetings and our general conversations became shorter. She was responding to other colleagues differently too, but we were all over-extended and too preoccupied to rally round.

I assumed she was tired. Nothing unusual about that in a hospital, after all. I never asked her directly what was going on, so I don't know. Maybe she had problems at home, or just decided to work less, and I would be doing her a disservice if I invented a reason for her withdrawal all these years later. What haunts me is that I noticed the change and didn't stop to ask why. She left the hospital soon after.

It has been revealed that doctors spend years learning to observe people. We study skin color, breathing, posture and movement. We become experts at listening to how people speak and notice when their account doesn't quite fit what we are seeing in front of us. Sometimes a tiny detail changes the direction of an examination.

I'm less certain that we are equally observant of the people working alongside us. Hospitals are notoriously busy places, and when someone continues to show up, doing good work and causing us no interruptions, our attention naturally goes elsewhere. This is particularly the case with competent people, and when we are so cocooned in our own work with all its decisions and distractions, it's not so easy to notice when a colleague interacts less or keeps their door closed. Any one of these signals could mean absolutely nothing, but if you know someone well enough to spot their behavior has changed, why not ask? I wish I had.

According to recent reports, years later, I came across a study by Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman, and Kipling Williams that made me reconsider that colleague. The researchers used brain imaging to study what happened when people experienced social exclusion during a virtual ball-tossing game. They found activity in some of the brain regions also involved in the distress of physical pain.

Industry observers note that the study was published in Science in 2003 and has since generated a good deal of research and discussion. A brain scan can't tell us what my colleague was experiencing, of course. I cannot say whether she felt personally excluded, though the study piqued my interest in something I had previously underestimated: how much being included matters to us.

You don't have to be physically alone to be lonely. I've known several people who have spent their lives elbow-deep in friends, family and colleagues, but who still feel disconnected from others. In a large hospital, and I'm sure in other workplaces, it's perfectly possible to speak to dozens of people every day, without enjoying a conversation where someone asks how you are and genuinely wants to hear the answer.

I used to believe that recognition was mainly about acknowledging exemplary work, but I'm no longer sure that's accurate. Praise has its place, and most of us like to hear what we did well, but in the difficult phases of my own life, the times I've felt truly noticed have been thanks to interactions that are much more subtle. Somebody maybe remembers a joke or a fact I told them weeks ago, or a colleague checks in when I'm unusually quiet. Occasionally a friend will hesitate and ask again after enquiring how I am and receiving the classic response 'Fine.'.

Sources indicate that none of these moments of recognition would appear in an organizational strategy. They cost nothing and can take less than a minute, but they tell us something valuable: someone has put their own busyness aside long enough to truly care.

Healthcare organizations spend time and money figuring out how to best care for patients, as they should. I wonder if we forget to look sideways at the people providing that care. Who pays attention to them? The people I worry about most aren't necessarily those who announce they're struggling. Often it's the person who just gets on with the job without complaining, who continues to do an excellent job while gradually becoming harder to reach.

It has been revealed that I still have no idea what happened to the consultant I worked alongside all those years ago. I only know that I noticed her withdrawal and attributed it to tiredness. If I found myself in the same situation today, I hope I would be attentive enough to knock on the door of her office, sit down and ask how she was, and actually wait long enough for the answer.

Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., & Williams, K. D. (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science, 302(5643), 290–292.

#63772. U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1325 w)
📖 Baca

U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.
  • The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S.
  • It has been revealed that “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, mentioned in a media briefing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S. for more than 12 months. On November 17, PAHO announced the end of the country’s measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.

It has been revealed that “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, mentioned in a media briefing. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.”.

PAHO’s review examined measles spread starting January 20, 2025, when the first person became ill in a large West Texas outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In a recent development, CDC data show 5,412 confirmed measles cases this year as of November 12. That’s the highest annual total since 1991 and more than double the 2025 count of 2,289 cases.

Andi Shane, MD, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, called the U.S. losing measles elimination status “a public health alarm that we are not being effective and we’re not controlling measles as well.”.

The measles virus is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can catch it in a room up to two hours after an infected person has left, according to the CDC.

“There’s really been very little measles in the United States over the past 25 years until January 2025,” William Moss, MD, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Healthline.

Losing the status itself doesn’t change much about daily life for most Americans, Moss stated. The concern is the measles outbreaks, hospitalizations and deaths behind the loss, he said.

He called the loss “a major red flag” after “enormous efforts over the past 26 years” to keep the status.

Industry observers note that A country loses its elimination status when there is “uninterrupted circulation of the same virus genotype and lineage for 12 months or more,” according to PAHO. Shane explained it this way: “For the past 12 months in the United States, we’ve had ongoing circulation of the measles virus and person-to-person transmission is occurring.”.

Canada lost its elimination status in November 2025, and the U.K. and five European countries lost theirs earlier in 2026.

The U.S. can regain the status. “Other countries have done that,” Moss remarked. Brazil, which lost its status in 2019, regained it in November 2024. Venezuela, which lost its status in 2018, regained it in 2023, according to PAHO.

Before the measles vaccine, measles infected an estimated 3 million to 4 million Americans each year, according to the CDC. Among reported cases, about 400 to 500 people died each year, 48,000 needed hospital care, and 1,000 developed encephalitis, or brain swelling.

Here’s a timeline of measles elimination in the U.S.:.

Moss noted elimination efforts “really intensified” after a large outbreak from 1989 to 1992. Part of that push was “really promoting school entry vaccination checks,” he said.

“That was one of the key policy changes that I think allowed for measles elimination in the United States.”.

Every state and Washington, D.C., require children to be vaccinated against measles to attend school, though exemptions vary by state, according to the nonprofit health policy organization KFF.

Fewer kindergartners are getting the MMR vaccine, according to the CDC.

Kindergarten MMR coverage fell from 95.2% in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. About 280,000 kindergartners started the 2025–2026 school year without records showing they had completed the MMR series, the CDC reported.

Shane said “95 out of 100 people need to be protected against measles” for a community to get herd protection.

“So since we’ve been below that for many, many months, that is also contributing to the loss of our elimination status,” she said.

“It takes two things to have a measles outbreak,” Moss stated. A community needs low vaccine coverage, and someone with measles has to enter it and “start the chain of transmission,” he said.

About 96% of this year’s cases were among people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, up from 93% in 2025, according to the CDC.

Moss said many of those cases are adults.

“This is particularly true in Pennsylvania, where about two-thirds of the cases are in adults,” he mentioned. Many never got vaccinated as kids and grew up while measles was rare, so they never built natural immunity, he said.

According to recent reports, he noted that having so many unvaccinated adults puts pregnant people and adults with chronic conditions like lung disease at risk of serious illness. The U.S. has already seen “dozens of pregnant women actually getting infected during pregnancy,” he remarked.Infected parents can also spread measles to young children and grandparents, Shane said. Shane traced much of the hesitancy to the pandemic. “With COVID there’s been an overall distrust in vaccines and vaccination that initially started with COVID but has now spread to other vaccines,” she said.

Moss pointed to the federal government. “We know what it takes to achieve and sustain elimination. We have the expertise. We have the resources,” he said.

He cited staff cuts at the CDC and remarked messaging from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Donald Trump has undermined vaccine confidence. He called federal messaging on vaccines “really mixed and weak.”.

Moss also criticized the President’s August 10 executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split into separate shots for each disease.

“There’s no justification for that, and those vaccines don’t even exist in the United States,” he said.

In a recent development, measles may cause ear infections, diarrhea, pneumonia, encephalitis and, in some cases, death, according to the CDC. The disease may also weaken the immune system for weeks to a year after recovery, raising the risk of flu, COVID-19, or RSV, Shane noted. “It’s not a benign childhood disease,” Moss said.

In a recent development, the best protection against measles is two doses of the MMR vaccine, which are about 97% effective, according to the CDC. Shane mentioned, “There are not very many other things we do in life that give you such great protection.” People who missed doses can still catch up, she added. “If you just don’t know or can’t tell, there’s no harm — as long as you’re eligible — in getting another MMR vaccine.”.

Shane added that “parents really want to do the right thing for their children.”.

Industry observers note that “We know that the MMR vaccine — that’s the vaccine that provides protection against measles — is a safe vaccine. It’s a very effective vaccine,” Shane said.

Babies under 12 months are too young for the vaccine. “So they depend on the protection of the people around them,” Shane said.

According to recent reports, the CDC recommends a first MMR dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at 4 to 6 years. Babies 6 to 11 months old who will travel internationally should get an early dose, and adults without proof of immunity should get at least one dose, according to the CDC.

Industry observers note that to stop the outbreaks, Moss noted the U.S. will need to “increase vaccine coverage, particularly in those communities that have had long-standing low vaccine rates.”.

Sources indicate that so far, the response has been “more reactive than proactive,” Moss said. Public health teams scramble once an outbreak starts, he said, and he wants more outreach to at-risk communities before measles arrives.

“I am worried about the ability of the United States to regain measles elimination status in the current climate,” Moss said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in March, we reported on a bobcat who endured a four-hour surgery on two broken legs after getting hit and dragged by a car, after her head had gotten stuck in the car’s grill.
  • “This is a very unusual case, as most animals that are hit by a tractor-trailer die due to their injuries or are killed instantly,” Tracie Young, director of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center tells Popular Science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in March, we reported on a bobcat who endured a four-hour surgery on two broken legs after getting hit and dragged by a car, after her head had gotten stuck in the car’s grill. During a strangely similar scenario, the same wildlife center in Pennsylvania recently treated a great horned owl (Bubo virginianus) who also got jammed in the front of a vehicle. But this one was dragged along for 70 miles.

“This is a very unusual case, as most animals that are hit by a tractor-trailer die due to their injuries or are killed instantly,” Tracie Young, director of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center tells Popular Science.

It has been revealed that the wildlife center’s team received a voicemail from cargo and freight organization Old Dominion Freight Line, saying that one of their drivers in Pennsylvania had hit an owl. When they called back, they discovered that the owl was alive and had gotten stuck in the truck’s air dam. The company’s maintenance team was able to remove the owl, but something was clearly wrong with the bird because it couldn’t fly away.

Industry observers note that the wildlife team told them to place the injured animal in a dark and quiet place. Ultimately, transport volunteers were able to transfer the owl to Raven Ridge, where the team had waited to receive the patient past the wildlife center’s closing hours. Its feathers were a mess, but the staff was shocked to find no broken wings or legs, nor open wounds. The owl had just injured its left eye.

Recent findings suggest that but when they called back the next day, “the story got even more incredible,” according to the wildlife center. The driver had felt the collision, but she didn’t know that the owl had gotten stuck on the truck, so she’d continued driving all the way back to the terminal.

Sources indicate that “The distance from the spot where the owl was hit to the terminal was 70 miles,” the team wrote.“The owl was stuck headfirst in the fiberglass air dam for 70 miles at 65 miles per hour. It’s truly the luckiest owl we’ve ever seen.”.

Staff brought the hardy survivor to their vet for an eye exam, which revealed blood and swelling in the injured eye. The wildlife team is now monitoring the bird’s recovery.

“The owl is doing great, and the left eye that sustained the damage is also healing. After we move the owl outside into a flight cage, we will make sure that the owl can sustain flight, that there are no obvious underlying concerns, and that it can find the food placed in its cage,” Young concludes.

The goal is to ultimately release it close to where the collision occurred.

#63767. Lived Experience and Epistemic Privilege

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1452 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Lived Experience and Epistemic Privilege

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Ich habe Lebenserfahrung [I have life experience]."—E.
  • "Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other."—Benjamin Franklin, 1743, meditating on the benefits of heeding advice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Recent findings suggest that "Ich habe Lebenserfahrung [I have life experience]."—E. Rudolf Krüger, putting his son in his place.

"Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other."—Benjamin Franklin, 1743, meditating on the benefits of heeding advice.

A current trend in the psychological scene is seeking to rehabilitate lived experience as an element of scholarship (Krueger, 2026). The importance of lived experience as part of the human condition is undeniable (Casey, 2023). It is also undeniable that there is value in sampling reports of lived experience widely to ensure that a broad spectrum of voices is being heard; indeed, there is also value in oversampling voices from small populations to ensure that minority views are not drowned out by a majority din (Kalsbeek, 2003).

There are good reasons to think, however, that a chorus of voices will not amount to scholarship unless it is tamed, disciplined, and critically examined. Scientific methods can do this. They impose standards on the collection, the organization, and the interpretation of evidence (Godwin & Goodwin, 2016). Although stories and narratives are obligatory elements of the human condition (Gottschall, 2012), they cannot replace science; they can only be objects of scientific study. Stories are data, that is, material to be curated by theory and explored with standardized methodology. The idea that stories of lived experience can stand on their own is as mistaken as the idea that quantitative data, and especially “significant data,” reveal reality all by themselves, without help from or intervention by a theoretically minded intellect (Felin et al., 2021).

Sir Karl Popper (1963) made this point jokingly. Beginning in 1928, he invited his students to “observe,” and when they asked, "What?" Popper exclaimed, "Aha!" Observation needs guidance. Then, the act of making an observation can create value; indeed, it can bring forth a reality, but only inasmuch as the observation is embedded in a web of expectations, knowledge, and prior experience. A phenomenologist might say that the lived experience of sensing and perceiving is the thing: It is Kant’s (1783) Ding an sich. We do not perceive a reality that is out there; instead, having a sensory experience is the reality.

Notable as they are, it is doubtful that lived experiences can supersede systematic scientific work. Yet, stories and narratives populate the literature. How do they get in? One pathway is for everyone so inclined to write up their story and get it published. This genre of literature exists. When asked, the AI engine Claude estimates the number of published biographies to exceed 10,000 annually. A search of the term "Google n-gram viewer" demonstrates that during the post-WWII era, the term “memoir” has risen in popularity, in tandem with the term self-esteem, suggesting a cultural drift to greater concern with the individual self. Yet, the term "memoir" already enjoyed an earlier flowering during the era of romanticism (see Figure 1).

According to recent reports, to see how stories and narratives of lived experience enter the psychological literature, we have to look to the pathways offered by the field of qualitative psychology. Here, an increasingly popular view is that both the conductors of qualitative research and their informants gain epistemic privilege from lived experience relevant to the subject matter at hand (Levitt & Pierorazio, 2026). This view is critical of investigative neutrality, a traditional value of the scientific mindset. Thomas Nagel (1986) referred to this mindset when asking whether we can take “a view from nowhere,” a perspective which privileges no one (also, Weber, 1904; 1917).

According to recent reports, of course, the lived experience of informants is critical when it underlies the expertise that needs to be brought to the investigation. When researching, for example, what the experience of post-traumatic stress is like, informants must be found who have had that experience. Insisting that researchers ought to have had that same type of experience would be an odd demand. At best, an investigator’s lived experience is irrelevant; at worst, it sets the stage for methodological bias.

The terms of lived experience and epistemic privilege are increasingly seen in the literature, as shown by the second n-gram graph (Figure 2). The relative popularity of the term epistemic privilege seems to be lagging, perhaps because this term is more difficult to comprehend. One reason for this difficulty is that the term has been used in more than one way. One usage is to refer to a knowledgeable person who has privileged access to the material under investigation. To the early school of introspective psychology, pioneered by Wilhelm Wundt, privileged access to one’s own mental contents was the foundation of their scientific efforts. A very different way of referring to epistemic privilege is political (e.g., Hartsock, 1983). Here, the position of the researcher is called into question (or “interrogated”) as a source of bias or perhaps even oppressive intent. Wundt is turned on his head.

According to recent reports, many authors feel strongly about critically assessing researchers’ epistemic privilege. Alas, limiting access to research outlets because of concerns regarding the researcher’s positionality sets up a slippery slope that can lead to unwarranted exclusion. It is worthwhile asking whether psychological science is not best served by an ethos of epistemic neutrality. Let the quality and rigor of the research speak for itself. This ethic allows authors of different positionality and authors with different kinds of epistemic privilege—or lack thereof—to contribute to the conversation. Authors in the progressive vein, for example, may wish to recall that from Marx to Lenin and to the Frankfurt School, the most influential authors emerged from the bourgeoisie. Should they have been denied the privilege of championing the interests of the proletariat?

My sympathies lie with the conventional ethic of blind reception. Let the research speak for itself, and let it be evaluated in light of explicit, rigorous, and shared standards. In my teaching, though, I seek to help students situate individual research articles within the authors’ life’s work. When students give a presentation in class, I ask them to include a short author biography with key data from their career and even a photo if they can find one. This exercise helps students understand why the researchers care about their work and see connections across studies. The goal is not to “interrogate” the researchers’ motives or use their demographic data as grounds for speculation about their intentions.

Robust scientific results should stand regardless of who produced them. In time, memory for findings should crystallize, while memory for the authors’ identity should suffer the fate of source amnesia. May the findings last—if they are true and replicable—while the finders’ identities fade.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Silicon anodes could be the next big thing in lithium-ion battery tech.
  • On Wednesday, Sila Nanotechnologies unveiled a new multi-year offtake agreement with Panasonic.
  • We've heard a lot about silicon-carbon batteries over the last few months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silicon anodes could be the next big thing in lithium-ion battery tech. A new deal paves the way for those more advanced batteries to be made in the U.S.

On Wednesday, Sila Nanotechnologies unveiled a new multi-year offtake agreement with Panasonic. Sila's role is to supply Panasonic with its silicon-carbon anode material, which the battery giant will use in its U.S. plants to build next-generation battery cells.

We've heard a lot about silicon-carbon batteries over the last few months. Mercedes-Benz bought into the idea, Porsche invested in it too. General Motors is going all-in on the tech, the automaker's battery chief, Kurt Kelty, told us earlier this year. So why the massive fuss?

Recent findings suggest that most lithium-ion batteries use graphite on the anode side. Sila's approach uses silicon, which can hold dramatically more lithium. In theory, that means a more energy-dense battery with no additional weight and faster charging speeds. A win all around.

But, there is a trade-off in the material. Silicon has a habit of "swelling" as it charges and ages due to the sheer amount of extra lithium it can absorb compared to graphite. Sila says its Titan Silicon anode solves this problem by reducing overall expansion to something more akin to traditional graphite-based anodes. Its anodes already help power some consumer electronics, like Whoop bands.

Sources indicate that the two companies have been working together to commercialize the tech since 2023 when Panasonic first unveiled plans to procure anode material from Sila. Now, Panasonic plans to procure it at scale.

According to recent reports, sila's facility in Washington was completed in later 2025 with the ability to produce around 2 Gigawatt-hours of battery material. That's enough to manufacture around 26,000 BEV batteries annually, based on a typical EV battery size of 75 kWh. In July, it secured funding to ramp production to up to 250 GWh. If all goes well, Sila notes that Panasonic has the option to offtake more than $1 billion in product over time.

Breaking: Tiny egg-eating snake discovered in Ethiopia

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (373 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Biologists have discovered multiple upcoming species of egg-eating snakes slithering through the forests near southeastern Ethiopia’s Bale Mountains.
  • “Three other species in this genus are still waiting in line,” Arthur Tiutenko, a study co-author and herpetologist at Germany’s Friedrich-Alexander University of Erlangen–Nuremberg (FAU), remarked in a statement.
  • It has been revealed that many snakes will snack on an egg if the opportunity presents itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Biologists have discovered multiple upcoming species of egg-eating snakes slithering through the forests near southeastern Ethiopia’s Bale Mountains. Although researchers only described the white-throated egg-eater (Dasypeltis albigularis) in their study recently published in the journal Herpetozoa, they promised that information on additional finds is on the way.

“Three other species in this genus are still waiting in line,” Arthur Tiutenko, a study co-author and herpetologist at Germany’s Friedrich-Alexander University of Erlangen–Nuremberg (FAU), remarked in a statement.

It has been revealed that many snakes will snack on an egg if the opportunity presents itself. But for a handful of species, it’s all eggs, all the time. These nonvenomous snakes solely eat shelled embryos, and largely exist in Africa and some portions of India. To devour their meals, egg-eating snakes have evolved a set of very clever biological tricks. First, their back bones extend all the way into their esophagus and function like a saw to slice open shells. From there, the snake’s neck muscles contract and funnel the egg contents down its throat. Once finished, the reptile simply spits out the cracked shells.

However, Tiutenko’s team almost missed D. albigularis entirely. At first glance, the snake looks extremely similar to a species called the montane egg-eater (Dasypeltis atra). A closer inspection revealed some key differences—a patch of white scales extending down its stomach earned its “white-throated” moniker, while the skin between each scale has a distinctly blue shimmer. Other egg-eating snakes can rub their scales to create a rustling noise that startles foes, but only the D. albigularis females do the same—and they do it silently.

Recent findings suggest that don’t envision python-sized snakes chowing down on chicken eggs though. D. albigularis is less than eight inches long, weighs only 0.05 ounces, and is about as thick as a knitting needle. This means the snakes only have eyes for particularly tiny eggs from various diminutive birds. Luckily, their regional home is full of options.

“That may also be the reason why egg-eating snakes only live in Africa, and in particular in a small area in the southwest corner of the Arabian peninsula,” added Tiutenko.

#63764. Latest Guidelines Recommend Routine Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Over 50
